blocks.prompt: The Seed That Sailed
blocks.text: A coconut is a seed. It is one of the biggest seeds in the world. Inside the hard shell is sweet water and food for a baby tree. Around the shell is a thick, dry husk. The husk is packed with air, so the coconut floats like a little boat. A coconut can drop off a palm tree into the sea. Waves carry it for weeks. The salt water cannot get in through the hard shell. At last a wave pushes the coconut up onto warm sand far away. The shell splits. A green shoot pushes up. Roots push down. Slowly, a new palm tree grows on a new island.

blocks.prompt: The Top of a Mountain
blocks.text: Look at a small island in a big ocean. It looks like a scoop of sand someone dropped on the water. It is not. Almost every island in the deep ocean is the top of a mountain. The rest of the mountain keeps going down, all the way to the sea floor thousands of feet below. You are seeing only the last few feet of something enormous. Many of those mountains are built by hot rock. In one spot under the Pacific Ocean, melted rock rises from deep inside Earth and pours out onto the sea floor. It cools and turns hard. More pours out on top of it. Over thousands of years the pile grows taller, until one day its top breaks through the waves, and a new island is born. Here is the strange part. The hot spot stays in one place, but the sea floor above it is moving. It slides along about as far as your hand is wide each year. So each island is slowly carried away from the hot spot that made it, and a new island starts growing behind it. That is why the Hawaiian Islands lie in a long line, like beads on a string.

from deep inside Earth, rising through a hot spot
about as far as your hand is wide
(inference: the hot spot stays still while the sea floor slides over it, so each island is carried away in turn)

blocks.prompt: The Loneliest Place on Earth
blocks.text: A brand new island is the loneliest place on Earth. It is bare rock and ash. Nothing grows. Nothing crawls. No seed, no ant, no bird. And yet, given enough time, it fills with life. Scientists have watched it happen from the very first day. In November 1963, fishermen off the south coast of Iceland saw smoke rising out of open ocean. Hot rock was pouring from the sea floor and piling up fast. Within days there was an island where there had been only water. They named it Surtsey. Then the scientists did something clever. They closed the island off. Almost nobody was allowed to land, so that life would arrive entirely on its own and nobody could argue that people had carried it there. Life came three ways: on the wind, on wings, and on the waves. In 1965, a single sea rocket plant was found growing on the shore, sprouted from a seed the ocean had delivered. Flies and spiders blew in on the wind. Seabirds landed to rest, and everything a seabird brings came with them, including seeds stuck to their feathers. In 1986, gulls began nesting, and the island changed quickly. Their droppings turned bare ash into real soil, and plants spread thickly around the colony. Willow bushes took hold in the 1990s. Today about seventy kinds of plants have been found on Surtsey, along with nesting birds, insects, and earthworms in the ground beneath them. Nobody planted any of it. The island simply waited, and life found it.

notes: Reef coral needs shallow, sunlit water
An atoll is a ring with no island inside
Darwin solved atolls in the 1830s
Cooling sea floor sags and sinks
Coral grows up as the mountain goes down
A 1952 drill hit buried rock 4,000 feet down

blocks.prompt: The Ring in the Ocean
blocks.text: Fly over the tropical Pacific and you will pass over rings. Each one is a thin circle of coral and sand wrapped around a calm blue lagoon, with deep ocean falling away on every side. There is no mountain in the middle. There is no peak, no hill, nothing at all in the center. Just a ring. These are atolls, and for a long time nobody could explain them. Here is the puzzle. The coral that builds reefs is an animal, and it can only live in shallow, sunlit water, roughly the top hundred feet. Deeper than that it is too dark and the coral dies. So a ring of coral cannot have grown up from a sea floor thousands of feet down. It must have started in the shallows. But if it started in the shallows, where did the shallow ground go? A young naturalist named Charles Darwin worked it out in the 1830s while sailing around the world, and he worked most of it out before he had ever seen an atoll up close. His idea went like this. Start with a new island, a steep mountain of cooled rock standing in warm water. Coral settles in the shallows around its shore and builds a reef that hugs the coastline. Now the island begins to sink. Old sea floor cools, grows heavier, and sags under the weight of the mountain riding on it, so slowly that no person would ever notice. The coral notices. Coral grows upward toward the light, keeping pace with the sinking, a fraction of an inch a year. The shoreline creeps inward, the reef stays where it is, and a lagoon opens between them. The island keeps going down. At last its final peak slips beneath the surface for good, and the only thing left in the sunlight is the coral that grew around it. A ring. An atoll is the outline of a mountain that is no longer there. It was a beautiful idea, and Darwin could not prove it. He said so himself, and he named the test: drill straight down through an atoll. If he was right, the drill would pass through thousands of feet of old coral and finally strike the buried mountain. Nobody could drill that deep in his lifetime. In 1952, seventy years after he died, engineers drilled into Enewetak Atoll in the Marshall Islands. They cut through more than four thousand feet of coral limestone. Then the drill hit dark stone. The mountain was down there, exactly where Darwin had put it.

notes: Islands: about 5% of Earth's land

Island giants: Komodo dragons reach 10 feet
Island dwarfs: three-foot elephants on Malta

MacArthur and Wilson, 1967

blocks.prompt: Cradles and Graveyards: Why Islands Break the Rules
blocks.text: Islands make up only about five percent of the land on Earth. That small share carries a wildly outsized amount of life: roughly one in five of all bird species, along with enormous numbers of plants and animals found nowhere else on the planet. Islands also account for around three quarters of the extinctions of birds, mammals, reptiles, and amphibians recorded since the year 1500. Islands are, at the same time, the best place on Earth to become a new species and the worst place to be one. Understanding why explains a great deal about how life works everywhere else. Start with arrival. To reach a remote island, a living thing has to cross open ocean: blown on the wind, carried on wings, floating on a raft of driftwood, or riding inside a bird. That filter is brutal, and more importantly it is uneven. Seeds, spiders, and birds pass it fairly often. Large mammals and freshwater fish almost never do. So an island never receives a fair sample of the mainland. It receives a lopsided one, and whoever gets there first finds a world with empty roles to fill, no competition, and often no predators at all. Then comes change. A finch that lands on an island with no woodpeckers may discover beetles under bark and, over many generations, evolve a bill suited to prying them out. Bodies rearrange too, and they do it in two opposite directions. Large animals on islands tend to shrink, because a small island cannot feed a large body: Sicily and Malta once had elephants only a little over three feet tall. Small animals tend to grow, because the predators that kept them small never made the crossing: the Komodo dragon reaches ten feet. Birds with no ground predators repeatedly stop flying, since flight is expensive and escape is unnecessary. Islands run this experiment over and over in isolation, which is exactly why Darwin's finches and Wallace's years among the Malay islands pushed both men toward the same conclusion. In 1967, Robert MacArthur and Edward O. Wilson pushed the thinking further. They argued that the number of species on an island settles at a balance between two rates: new species arriving, and resident species dying out. Larger islands hold more, because they offer more room and more kinds of habitat. Closer islands hold more, because arrival is easier. That balance turned out to describe far more than islands in the sea. It fits any patch of habitat ringed by something a species cannot cross: a forest surrounded by farmland, a cold mountaintop, a park in a city. Their island theory became a tool for the whole planet. Now the graveyard. Everything that makes an island a cradle also makes it fragile. The species are few, the populations are small, the ranges are tiny, and they evolved in a world with no rats, no cats, and no goats. When ships arrived, that world ended in a hurry. The dodo, a large flightless pigeon on Mauritius, was gone within about a century of the first Dutch sailors landing. It was not simply eaten to death. The greater killers were the pigs and rats and monkeys that came ashore with the ships and ate its eggs off the open ground, because a dodo had never needed to hide a nest. An animal with no defenses is not stupid. It is an animal answering the question its island asked, and the question changed. The hopeful part is that island stories can run backward. Because islands are small and bounded, they are one of the few places where the damage can actually be undone. Clearing rats off a single island has brought entire seabird colonies back, sometimes within a few years. South Georgia, long overrun by rats that arrived on sealing and whaling ships, was declared rodent free in 2018 after an enormous clearing effort, and its birds are returning. Islands taught us how species are made. They may also be where we learn how to stop losing them.
